hook.text: Draw any backend, and every arrow between two boxes is an API: one side asks, the other answers, and both must agree on how. The interview tests whether you can design that agreement to be predictable, consistent, and hard to misuse.

hook-blog.text: Most answers here use one example, the page's own: a blog, with articles and their comments.

plan.text: Sixteen questions. Ten are worked through, and six go quickly at the end.

rest.text: Question one. What makes an API RESTful? It models the domain as resources, each with a URL, and acts on them with the standard HTTP methods.
rest.spoken: Question one. What makes an API restful? It models the domain as resources, each with a URL, and acts on them with the standard HTTP methods.

rest-nouns.text: So paths are nouns, like articles slash forty-two, never a verb like get article. Each request carries everything the server needs, with no session kept between requests. And methods and status codes mean what HTTP says they mean.

rest-why.text: Done well, a developer can guess the next endpoint. And because no request depends on the last, any server behind a load balancer can answer the next one.

methods.text: Question two. Walk through the main HTTP methods and their semantics. Two properties sort them. Safe: the server's state doesn't change. Idempotent: repeating the request has the same effect as sending it once.

methods-list.text: GET reads, and is both. PUT replaces a whole resource, and DELETE removes one: both idempotent. POST submits data to be processed, like a new article, and is neither. PATCH changes part of a resource, and isn't necessarily idempotent.

methods-delete.text: Two follow-ups. A second delete may answer not found, a different response, but the article is gone either way, so delete is still idempotent: the property is about state, not the reply.

methods-patch.text: And a patch that sets the status to published is idempotent. One that adds one to a view count is not.

codes.text: Question three. What do the HTTP status code classes mean? The first digit tells the story. Two hundreds succeed: two hundred OK, two oh one created, two oh four no content. Three hundreds redirect. Four hundreds blame the client, and five hundreds the server.

codes-why.text: The right code lets a client handle a failure in code, instead of parsing an error message.

authn.text: Question four. Four oh one versus four oh three, what is the difference?

authn-401.text: Four oh one, unauthorized, is really about authentication: the request has no valid credentials, and the response carries a challenge header saying how to authenticate.

authn-403.text: Four oh three, forbidden, means the server understood the request and refuses it. The credentials may be fine; they just aren't enough, and logging in again won't necessarily help.

authn-404.text: The follow-up: some APIs answer four oh four instead, on purpose, so a stranger can't learn that the resource exists.

idem.text: Question five. What is idempotency, and why does it matter for APIs? An idempotent operation has the same result whether it runs once or many times.

idem-retry.text: It matters because networks fail. A client that times out can't tell whether its request arrived, so it retries.

idem-run.text: Here's a payment of fifty dollars, sent with POST, which HTTP doesn't make idempotent. The first attempt is charged but its response is lost, and the client retries twice. Three charges: a hundred and fifty dollars.

idem-key.text: The fix is an idempotency key: a unique ID the client generates once and sends with every attempt. The server stores it with the payment. Each retry finds the key, inserts nothing, and gets the original payment back. Three requests, one charge.

idem-race.text: What makes it safe is a unique constraint on the key: even two retries racing each other can't both get in, because the database refuses the second.

page.text: Question six. How do you paginate a large collection? The simple way is offset and limit: skip forty, take twenty. It can jump to any page, but the database walks every row it skips.

page-cost.text: Run it in Postgres, the open-source relational database, on a hundred thousand articles, newest first. Page one reads twenty rows. Page five hundred reads ten thousand to return twenty, and page five thousand reads all hundred thousand.

page-drift.text: It can also repeat rows. A reader takes page one, a new article is published, and page two starts with the article page one ended on.

page-cursor.text: Cursor pagination hands back an opaque cursor marking where the page stopped, here the last article's ID. The next request asks for what comes after it: twenty rows read at any depth, and nothing shifts when articles arrive.

page-cost-two.text: It costs two things: no jumping straight to page five hundred, and an order that's unique and never changes, so a sort by time adds the ID as a tiebreaker.

auth.text: Question seven. Sessions versus JWT versus OAuth, how do they relate? They answer different questions.
auth.spoken: Question seven. Sessions versus JWT versus oh-auth, how do they relate? They answer different questions.

auth-session.text: With a session, the server stores the login and hands the client an opaque ID, usually in a cookie: forty-three random characters that mean nothing without the server's store.

auth-jwt.text: JWT, a JSON Web Token, is a signed format for claims. This one is a hundred sixty-four characters, and anyone can read it: decode the middle part, and there's the user, the role, and the expiry. The signature proves who issued it: change the role to admin, and it no longer verifies.
auth-jwt.spoken: JWT, a jay-son Web Token, is a signed format for claims. This one is a hundred sixty-four characters, and anyone can read it: decode the middle part, and there's the user, the role, and the expiry. The signature proves who issued it: change the role to admin, and it no longer verifies.

auth-oauth.text: OAuth isn't a token format at all. It's a framework for delegated authorization: letting one app reach your data on another service without your password. Its access tokens may be JWTs or opaque strings.
auth-oauth.spoken: Oh-auth isn't a token format at all. It's a framework for delegated authorization: letting one app reach your data on another service without your password. Its access tokens may be JWTs or opaque strings.

revoke.text: Question eight. When would you choose stateful sessions over stateless JWTs?

revoke-session.text: When you need instant revocation, to log a user out or ban them now, and can afford a session store every server shares. Delete the session, and the next request fails. Checked locally, a JWT stays valid until it expires, unless every check does a lookup again.

revoke-jwt.text: JWTs fit many services verifying requests without asking a session store each time.

revoke-hybrid.text: The common hybrid pairs a short-lived access token, say fifteen minutes, with a longer-lived refresh token that can be revoked. A banned user then keeps access for at most those fifteen minutes.

limit.text: Question nine. How do you rate-limit an API, and how should clients learn their limits? The server caps requests per client per window, commonly with a token bucket, which allows short bursts. Part two, on scaling, covers how it counts.

limit-contract.text: The client's half is a contract in the response. Over the limit, the answer is four twenty-nine, too many requests. Headers carry the rest: the limit, what's remaining, when the window resets, and Retry-After, how long to wait.

limit-client.text: A well-behaved client watches what's remaining, and slows down before it's refused. On a four twenty-nine, it waits at least Retry-After. Refused again, it doubles the wait each time, plus random jitter, so a crowd of clients doesn't return at once.

limit-safe.text: The same backoff serves timeouts and server errors, but there the client can't know what happened, so it repeats only what's safe: a GET, a PUT, or a POST with an idempotency key.

styles.text: Question ten. REST versus GraphQL versus gRPC, when does each fit?
styles.spoken: Question ten. Rest versus GraphQL versus gRPC, when does each fit?

styles-rest.text: REST is resources over HTTP and JSON: universally understood, easy to cache, the safe default for a public API. But a screen that needs an article, its author and its comments may make three round trips, and get fields it never shows.
styles-rest.spoken: Rest is resources over HTTP and jay-son: universally understood, easy to cache, the safe default for a public API. But a screen that needs an article, its author and its comments may make three round trips, and get fields it never shows.

styles-graphql.text: GraphQL lets the client ask for exactly the fields it wants, in one query, which suits rich, varied front ends. But caching and rate limiting get harder, and one query can be expensive, so a limit has to weigh what a query costs.

styles-grpc.text: gRPC sends binary Protocol Buffers over HTTP two: fast, strongly typed, and able to stream. It's ideal between internal services, with weaker browser support, and messages that aren't human-readable.

styles-mix.text: So a common design uses REST for the public API and gRPC between its own services.
styles-mix.spoken: So a common design uses rest for the public API and gRPC between its own services.

rapid-in.text: Six more, a sentence or two each.

r-naming.text: Name resources with plural nouns for collections and IDs for members: articles, article forty-two, its comments beneath it. No verbs in paths: the method is the verb. An action like publish becomes a state change: patch the status to published.

r-blog.text: So the blog is two collections: GET and POST on articles, GET, PATCH and DELETE on one article, GET and POST on its comments. Filters go in the query string, and a create answers two oh one, with a Location header pointing at the new article.

r-version.text: Version an API to protect clients from breaking changes, like removing a field or changing its type. A version in the path, slash v one, is the most visible and the pragmatic default. Adding an optional field needs no new version.

r-errors.text: Errors get the right status code and a consistent body: a stable code a client can branch on, a message for a person, and details per field. Never a stack trace.

r-hateoas.text: HATEOAS, hypermedia as the engine of application state, means responses carry links to what the client can do next. REST as first defined requires it; in practice most APIs skip it, though a link to the next page is common.
r-hateoas.spoken: Hate-ee-oss, hypermedia as the engine of application state, means responses carry links to what the client can do next. Rest as first defined requires it; in practice most APIs skip it, though a link to the next page is common.

r-content.text: Content negotiation lets one URL serve several representations: Accept says what the client can take, and Content-Type what it got. Encoding works the same way: ask for gzip, and this page of twenty articles arrives at about a sixth of its size.

next.text: Behind every one of these endpoints, the data has to live somewhere. Next: databases.
